# Aesthetic, muscle, and dermatologic effects of medical weight management: patient-reported outcomes shape a holistic preventive procedural approach

**Authors:** Kathyana P Santiago Mangual; Isabella Midura; Eryn Patin; Saroja Rao; Leon I Igel; Katherine H Saunders; Jocelyn Carter; Arianne S Kourosh

**Affiliations:** a Department of Dermatology, Yale School of Medicine, New Haven, Connecticut | b Department of Dermatology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts | c Department of Dermatology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts | d University of Texas Southwestern Medical School, Dallas, Texas | e Wake Forest School of Medicine, Winston-Salem, North Carolina | f Comprehensive Weight Control Center, Division of Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism, Weill Cornell Medicine, New York City, New York | g FlyteHealth, New Canaan, Connecticut | h Division of General Internal Medicine, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts | i Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts | j Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts

## Abstract

As glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have become increasingly central to obesity care, calls for protocols to mitigate or prevent potential aesthetic and muscle sequelae have emerged.

This study aimed to to evaluate patient-reported concerns regarding aesthetic and muscle-related changes during pharmacologic weight management, particularly among individuals treated with GLP-1RAs, and to highlight potential strategies to address these effects.

An institutional review board–approved anonymous survey of 1,226 patients receiving pharmacologic weight management through a national telemedicine platform assessed patient-reported dermatologic, aesthetic, and muscle-related outcomes. Survey findings were analyzed and supplemented with a targeted PubMed literature review to develop a practical management framework.

Over 60% of participants reported concerns including skin laxity, facial volume loss, hair shedding, worsened skin quality, and reduced muscle strength. These concerns increased with greater weight loss and were more common among GLP-1RA users, who generally experienced greater weight reduction than non-GLP-1RA users.

Limitations of this study include the voluntary survey design, potential selection and recall bias, and a study population largely consisting of White, female telemedicine patients, which may limit generalizability. Rate of weight loss was not captured, leaving its impact on outcomes uncertain.

As unwanted aesthetic and muscle effects can undermine treatment adherence, a holistic approach including nutrition, strength preservation, and – when appropriate – aesthetic and regenerative therapies – could promote improved weight and health outcomes.

Keywords: alopecia, GLP-1, poor skin quality, skin sagging, volume loss, weight loss

## What is known about this subject in regard to women and their families?

- Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists have become increasingly utilized in obesity care, and women comprise a large number of patients navigating weight management.

- Aesthetic, dermatologic, and muscle sequelae of patients treated with this pharmacotherapy for weight management have not been systematically evaluated by board-certified dermatologists in collaboration with weight management physicians.

## What is new from this article as messages for women and their families?

- Our study explores patient-reported dermatologic, muscle, and aesthetic concerns among patients using glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists.

- Our study offers a preventive, holistic approach to nutrition, strength preservation, and aesthetic and dermatologic therapies to optimize weight and health outcomes for patients undergoing treatment with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists.

## Introduction

The term “Ozempic face” has become emblematic of facial volume changes thought to be secondary to glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) use.1 Despite increasing recognition in social and clinical contexts, data on the prevalence and impact of dermatologic, muscle, and aesthetic effects remain limited.

This study, which evaluates patient-reported dermatologic, muscle, and aesthetic outcomes among individuals treated with weight management pharmacotherapy, informs prevention and management approaches. By emphasizing nutritional optimization, strength preservation, early dermatologic evaluation, and potential intervention, we propose integrating a preventive holistic framework that optimizes dermatologic, muscle, and aesthetic outcomes into the overall algorithm of weight management treatment.

## Materials and methods

This institutional review board–approved study utilized a voluntary, anonymous survey developed based on qualitative interviews with weight management physicians and dermatologists treating dermatologic concerns associated with weight management. This survey was made available in April-May 2025 to individuals receiving weight management treatment through a national telemedicine platform. Data collected included current weight management therapies: medication type, dosage, and duration, as well as pre-treatment and current body weight. Participants responded to qualitative items regarding dermatologic, muscle, and aesthetic outcomes associated with weight management therapy, such as changes in pre-existing skin conditions, emergence of new conditions, and perceived changes in skin quality, hair, nails, facial appearance, and body composition.

Study data were collected and analyzed using Research Electronic Data Capture. A targeted literature review using PubMed was conducted to identify evidence-based strategies for preventing and managing the most frequently reported dermatologic and aesthetic effects. These findings were synthesized into a practical framework for use in dermatologic practice.

## Results

A total of 1,226 participants completed the survey. Demographic characteristics, treatment details, and weight management outcomes are summarized in Table 1. Participants were categorized into 4 treatment cohorts based on whether their current weight management regimen included a GLP-1-RA, and stratified into weight loss cohorts according to percentage total body weight loss (TBWL).

Among respondents, 61.9% reported at least one dermatologic, muscle, or aesthetic concern: skin sagging (37.7%), facial volume loss (29.2%), hair loss (28.9%), worsened skin quality (increased dryness and/or fine lines and wrinkles) (24.1%), decreased muscle strength (17.9%), with a majority of participants reporting more than one concern (Fig. 1).

*Fig. 1.: Self-reported dermatologic, muscle, and aesthetic effects of medical weight management.*

Graphical analysis of these concerns in relation to both TBWL and treatment cohort revealed 2 trends (Fig. 2). Independent of treatment modality, the proportion of participants reporting concerns increased with greater TBWL. In addition, for most concerns, a higher proportion of participants receiving GLP-1RA-based therapy reported concerns compared with those not on GLP-1RA-based therapy.

*Fig. 2.: Self-reported dermatologic, muscle, and aesthetic effects as functions of treatment modality and total body weight loss. GLP-1, glucagon-like peptide-1; TBWLC, total body weight loss cohort; TC, treatment cohort.*

Consistent with these trends, most participants (90.9%) who achieved >20% TBWL reported at least one concern, compared with 50.5% of those who achieved <10% TBWL. Furthermore, a greater proportion of participants receiving GLP-1RA therapy reported at least one concern compared with those not on GLP-1 therapy. The greatest difference was observed when comparing participants who achieved 10-20% TBWL: 76.6% in the GLP-1RA cohort reported at least one concern, versus 52.1% in the non-GLP-1RA cohort.

## Discussion

In this survey of over 1,200 individuals undergoing medical weight management, aesthetic, muscle, and dermatologic concerns were common. Participants who achieved >20% TBWL reported higher rates of concerns compared with those achieving <10% TBWL, suggesting a dose-response relationship. Concerns were more frequent among patients treated with GLP-1-RAs.

### Skin sagging

Skin sagging, particularly of the arms (71%, n = 390), was the most frequently reported concern. Weight loss limits the skin’s adaptive capacity, leading to laxity in the face, neck, arms, abdomen, and thighs. Loss of elastin, collagen, and subcutaneous fat produces wrinkles, folds, and drooping that diminish aesthetic gains and may cause functional limitations.2,3

Nonsurgical options for mild to moderate laxity include radiofrequency (RF), high-intensity focused ultrasound, fractional lasers, and fractional RF microneedling, which stimulate collagen and elastin synthesis to improve firmness and elasticity with minimal downtime.4–6

### Decreased facial volume

Nearly one third of participants reported facial volume loss, particularly among those with >20% weight loss and on GLP-1-RAs. The most affected regions are typically the midface, temples, and periorbital area, where subcutaneous fat depletion produces a hollow, aged appearance.1,3 Researchers hypothesize GLP-1RAs cause a loss of protective cytokines, increase oxidative stress, and promote adipose-derived stem cell death.7

Treatment includes dermal fillers and biostimulatory agents such as poly-L-lactic acid and calcium hydroxylapatite to promote longer-term collagen production. Early initiation of poly-L-lactic acid during medical weight management may help prevent progression of volume loss.8

### Alopecia

Alopecia was reported by 29% of participants, particularly among those with >20% weight loss and on GLP-1RA therapy. While GLP-1RAs may improve scalp perfusion, they may also disrupt the follicular cycle, contributing to telogen effluvium.9 Nutritional deficiencies and caloric restriction further exacerbate shedding.10 Conversely, there is evidence to suggest GLP-1RAs mitigate inflammation and fibrosis in central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia, thus improving clinical outcomes for these patients.11

Alopecia often improves with nutritional recovery and weight stabilization in patients with telogen effluvium, although data in GLP-1RA users are lacking. Preventive strategies include adequate protein and micronutrient intake, as well as topical or oral minoxidil. For patients with androgenetic alopecia, 5α-reductase and androgen receptor blockade can be considered after discussion with their physician about other considerations (eg, possible side effects). Early initiation of platelet-rich-plasma therapy can be recommended for high-risk patients.12–14

### Worsened skin quality

Approximately one fourth of participants reported worsened skin quality, most often dryness with new fine lines and wrinkles, particularly among those with >20% weight loss. Contributing factors might include reduced hydration from medication-related thirst suppression, and protein or micronutrient deficits during weight loss. Dehydration and micronutrient deficiencies – including depletion of water-soluble vitamins such as vitamin C and copper (its deficiency implicated in genodermatoses with premature aging) – can have a compounded effect that compromises hydration, collagen synthesis, and barrier function, leading to xerosis, poor healing, and reduced elasticity.15–19 Histologic studies following massive weight loss (38-68 kg) have demonstrated epidermal thinning, disorganization of collagen, and fragmentation of elastic fibers.20,21

Prevention focuses on nutritional optimization to ensure adequate fluid and protein intake and to avoid nutritional deficiencies. Additional management may include use of retinoids, antioxidants, microdepot hyaluronic acid injections (United States Food and Drug Administration-approved to improve skin smoothness), and energy-based procedures such as lasers, microneedling, and RF.15,22

### Decreased muscle strength

Eighteen percent of participants reported decreased muscle strength, mostly involving the extremities. While GLP-1RAs primarily reduce fat mass, 15-25% of weight loss is lean tissue; however, volume loss is not reflective of function or strength.23,24 Lean tissue loss may be exacerbated by rapid weight reduction, inadequate protein intake, and insufficient resistance training. Excessive muscle depletion raises risks for sarcopenia, functional decline, and even longevity, with low thigh muscle strength predicting poorer survival.16,25

Preservation requires optimizing nutrition and resistance training, particularly targeting the thigh muscles.23,25 Adjunctive energy-based technologies such as high-intensity focused electromagnetic therapy can improve muscle tone.16,26,27 Early preventive measures are essential to maintain muscle strength and function during weight loss.

This study highlights the importance of anticipating potential dermatologic, muscle, and aesthetic sequelae of medical weight management, particularly in the setting of significant TBWL, as these concerns can affect weight and health outcomes. A multidisciplinary approach is essential to balance metabolic and aesthetic goals. Collaboration among obesity medicine specialists, dietitians, and medical and cosmetic dermatologists facilitates early identification of at-risk patients and implementation of preventive measures.

Foundational measures include proactive counseling, adequate protein intake, micronutrient sufficiency, hydration, and resistance exercise. Dermatologic and aesthetic interventions include procedural options like energy-based therapies, fillers, and platelet-rich-plasma, in addition to retinoids, antioxidants, emollients, and topical and oral minoxidil (Table 2).

Limitations of this study include the voluntary survey design, potential selection and recall bias, and a study population largely consisting of White, female telemedicine patients, which may limit generalizability. Rate of weight loss was not captured, leaving its impact on muscle, dermatologic, and aesthetic outcomes uncertain; this represents an area for future research.

## Conclusion

While medical weight management offers significant health benefits, it is frequently accompanied by aesthetic, muscle, and dermatologic concerns that can limit adherence to treatment. As the use of GLP-1-RAs expands and patients can achieve greater TBWL, aesthetic, muscle, and dermatologic impacts will become more prevalent. A holistic approach to caring for these patients, inclusive of their dermatologic, muscle, and aesthetic needs, is necessary to promote greater weight and health outcomes.
